title: Druxt Auth 0.5.0; two ways to sign in without leaving your site
description: Signing into a decoupled Drupal site has meant a trip to Drupal and back. Druxt Auth 0.5.0 lets a Nuxt front end take the username and password on its own form instead, two different ways, and neither shows the visitor a page that isn't yours.

content.html: Signing someone into a decoupled Drupal site has usually meant sending them away to do it. They click sign in, the browser leaves for Drupal, they meet Drupal's login page and then a consent screen, and eventually they land back where they started. 0.5.0 adds two ways to take the username and password on your own form instead.

Both keep the visitor on your site the whole way through, and neither shows them a page that isn't yours. Which one you want depends on whether you can hold a secret on the server, and whether Drupal's own screens need to know who is looking.

content.alt: The druxtjs.org getting-started tutorial with a Sign in to edit dialog open over it, asking for a username and password
content.caption: Signing in happens on the page you were reading. The dialog says it plainly: reading the docs never needs an account.

content.html: The first is the authorization code grant you already had, handed credentials. Druxt Auth signs the visitor in through Drupal's JSON login first, so the authorize step finds a session already waiting and returns a code without rendering anything:

content.title: pages/sign-in.vue
content.highlighted: await $auth.loginWith('drupal-authorization_code', { credentials: { name, pass }, })

content.html: You get a real Drupal session out of that, which matters if you proxy Drupal's own pages for editors, and logout() ends it again. No client secret goes anywhere near the app, because underneath it is still authorization code with PKCE.
The second is the password grant. Credentials go to Drupal's token endpoint through Druxt Auth's own server route, so the Nuxt site has to be rendering on a server:

content.title: pages/sign-in.vue
content.highlighted: await $auth.loginWith('drupal-password', { data: { username, password }, })

content.html: This one hands back tokens and nothing else. Drupal's own pages stay anonymous under it however signed in the frontend looks, which surprises you at first. Set passwordSession and the sign-in opens a Drupal session too, with logout() ending both.
Neither needs a form from you. 0.5.0 ships a DruxtAuthLogin component and a page at /user/login, which a site replaces by dropping its own component of that name into components/.

Both of these post credentials to an endpoint. Drupal's JSON login for the first, the token endpoint for the second. Neither runs Drupal's login form, and a fair amount of Drupal's login behaviour lives on that form rather than behind it.

Drupal's tfa module interposes there. So does a forced password change, a terms gate, and anything else that alters the login form. Skip the form and you skip those with it. Core's own checks inside the auth controller, flood control among them, should still apply, though check that rather than take my word for it.

None of that makes the credential options wrong. It makes them a trade, because the trip to Drupal is what ran whatever the login form enforced. If you need two factor the redirect is still there, and calling loginWith without credentials asks for it. I have run two factor on a decoupled front end elsewhere and it works. The experience is not pretty yet, and making it pretty is on my list.

paragraphs.title: What the login form was doing for you

content.html: Origin is the first. The session cookie from that JSON login has to reach the authorize request, so Drupal and the frontend must look like one site to the browser, which Druxt's API proxy arranges. Subdomains work once the endpoints point at Drupal and CORS allows credentials. Across separate domains the cookie would be third party, so the credential options are out and the redirect is the only way in.

Consumers are the second. The browser flow takes a public Consumer with no secret, the password grant a confidential one, and a Consumer cannot be both. A site running both needs two, with passwordClientId for the second. It also has to authorise automatically, or the authorize step shows Drupal's consent page and the visitor sees Drupal anyway.

A Drupal session already open in the browser is also refused, rather than quietly signing the visitor in as whoever left it there. The error sets sessionInUse so your form can explain itself. To end it instead, point sessionLogout at a route on your backend, which you write, because core cannot end a session it never issued a logout token for.

paragraphs.title: Two things that catch people out

content.html: druxtjs.org is the example I have been testing against, with the password grant on a branch there rather than in production. The site was rebuilt this month so Druxt renders its own docs, every docs page a node and the navigation a menu, with a playground that renders the core components against the Umami demo or any Drupal you paste in.

content.alt: A phone screen showing the sign-in dialog, credentials entered, then the tutorial page with an avatar in the header and an editor bar along the bottom
content.caption: The password grant on a phone, start to finish, with no navigation in between. The bar along the bottom is the editing work this is being built for.

content.html: Plenty is queued behind it. Druxt core has unreleased fixes waiting on 0.25.0, the editor bar is still being drawn, and in-page editing is built against it. Documentation and examples were the biggest blocker on 1.0.0, and they are done.

The password grant was never Druxt Auth's to give. Simple OAuth 6 removed it, on the reasoning that OAuth's best practices had moved on, and only Drupal's OAuth server can mint a token. Without something on the backend putting that grant back, the second option does not exist at all.

That something is Simple OAuth Password Grant, written by Christian Foidl. He made the first commit in February 2023 and has written almost all of it since, with Matthew Grasmick alongside. Install it, enable Password on the Consumer's grant types, and Druxt Auth's password strategy has something to talk to. Thank you both.

So which one do you want? Mine is the password grant, because it is the flow I wanted back when Simple OAuth dropped it. The authorization code option is probably the safer of the two, and the one that leaves a door open for two factor, so I would not tell you to copy me.

paragraphs.title: The module that makes the password grant possible

content.description: Druxt Auth, and the example app that runs both flows against a real Drupal. Sponsorship is what keeps Druxt maintained.
